coverage: Both full English editions, 28 scenes and 895 paragraphs. Speaking parts, named people, spirits, gods and devils, and the figures the dialogue names. Places are not cast.

entities.name: Faust
entities.body: The scholar who has read everything and knows nothing worth knowing, and signs away his soul for one moment he would want to keep. The wager is his own idea, and so is its wording.

entities.name: Mephistopheles
entities.body: The devil who bets the Lord that he can have Faust, and then finds that ruining him is harder than it looked. He calls himself the spirit that always denies, and he is the funniest thing in the play.

entities.name: Margaret
entities.body: Gretchen: a girl of fourteen or fifteen who has never been outside her own street. What Faust does to her is the whole second half of the play, and the last word on her is not his.

entities.name: The Lord
entities.body: God in the Prologue in Heaven, who lets Mephistopheles have his wager because a man’s striving needs a companion who goads.

entities.name: The Spirit of the Earth
entities.body: The power Faust conjures and cannot bear to look at, which tells him he resembles the spirit he can grasp — and not this one.

entities.name: Martha
entities.body: Margaret’s neighbour, a widow who is not much troubled about her missing husband and is very ready to be courted by Mephistopheles.

entities.name: Valentine
entities.body: Margaret’s brother, a soldier, who used to be proud of her name and dies in the street outside her door cursing it.

entities.name: Bessy
entities.body: The neighbour at the well who tells Margaret, with relish, what has happened to Barbara — not knowing she is describing Margaret’s own future.

entities.name: The Evil Spirit
entities.body: The voice behind Margaret in the cathedral, which asks her how things stood when she was still innocent.

entities.name: Barbara
entities.body: The girl in the next street who was got with child and abandoned; Bessy tells the story to Margaret without seeing what it means.

entities.name: Agatha
entities.body: A girl at the city gate, called away by her friend so as not to be seen with fortune-tellers.

entities.name: Catherine
entities.body: The girl in Mephistopheles’s serenade under Margaret’s window, warned not to go in to her lover as a maiden.

entities.name: The King in Thule
entities.body: The faithful king of the song Margaret sings while she undresses, who kept his dead love’s golden cup until he died.

entities.name: The Mater Dolorosa
entities.body: The image of the Virgin in the wall of the Zwinger, with flowers before it, that Margaret prays to.

entities.name: Wagner
entities.body: Faust’s assistant, entirely content with books and eager to be told he is making progress. Goethe uses him to show what Faust might have settled for.

entities.name: The Student
entities.body: The freshman who comes for advice and is sent off by Mephistopheles, in Faust’s gown, with a course of study designed to ruin him — and an autograph that reads "you shall be as gods, knowing good and evil."

entities.name: The Poodle
entities.body: The black dog that follows Faust home from the walk and turns out to be the devil; Faust spends a whole scene talking to it before it changes shape.

entities.name: Nostradamus
entities.body: The astrologer whose book of signs Faust opens, and in which he finds the sign of the Macrocosm and then the sign of the Earth Spirit.

entities.name: Frosch
entities.body: One of the four drinkers in Auerbach’s Cellar, and the one who tries hardest to keep the party going.

entities.name: Brander
entities.body: A drinker in Auerbach’s Cellar, who sings the song about the rat that ate poison.

entities.name: Siebel
entities.body: A drinker in Auerbach’s Cellar, unlucky in love and the first to grab for Mephistopheles’s throat.

entities.name: Altmayer
entities.body: The fourth drinker in Auerbach’s Cellar, and the soberest of them.

entities.name: The Witch
entities.body: The keeper of the kitchen where Faust is made thirty years younger; she recognises Mephistopheles at once and is scolded for using his old names.

entities.name: The Monkeys
entities.body: The witch’s household, who mind the cauldron, play with a crown and a glass ball, and beg for money.

entities.name: Helen
entities.body: The face in the witch’s mirror — Mephistopheles promises that with the drink in him Faust will see her in every woman.

entities.name: Cupid
entities.body: Named by Mephistopheles for what the philtre will do.

entities.name: Raphael
entities.body: The first of the three archangels in the Prologue in Heaven, who sings of the sun and its brother spheres.

entities.name: Gabriel
entities.body: The second archangel of the Prologue, who sings of the earth turning between splendour and night.

entities.name: Michael
entities.body: The third archangel of the Prologue, who sings of the storms raging from sea to land.

entities.name: The Three
entities.body: The archangels singing together, closing the Prologue’s hymn before Mephistopheles speaks.

entities.name: The Manager
entities.body: In the Prelude on the Stage, the one who wants a full house and tells the Poet what an audience actually is.

entities.name: The Poet
entities.body: In the Prelude, the one who refuses to write for the crowd and is told he will have to.

entities.name: The Merryman
entities.body: In the Prelude, the comic actor, who sides with neither and tells them both to get on with it.

entities.name: The townsfolk at the gate
entities.body: Goethe’s crowd on Easter Sunday, speaking in anonymous voices — mechanics choosing a tavern, servant-girls, burghers glad of a war far away in Turkey, a beggar, a soldier, a citizen’s daughter warned off the fortune-teller. None of them is named, and that is the point: this is the world Faust cannot be content with.

entities.name: The Old Peasant
entities.body: The villager who brings Faust the first draught, because Faust’s father worked among them in the plague year — the thanks that makes Faust confess what his father’s medicine actually did.

entities.name: Faust’s father
entities.body: The dark man of honour who brewed the red lion and the lily in his laboratory and killed more patients than the plague; Faust says so while accepting their gratitude.

entities.name: Luther
entities.body: Named only for his paunch, in Brander’s song about the rat.

entities.name: Mr Hans of Rippach
entities.body: A stock joke — the man from Rippach who does not exist, whom Mephistopheles is asked whether he supped with.

entities.name: Jack Rake
entities.body: The name Margaret’s type of admirer is given: a man who covets every flower for himself.

entities.name: The Will-o’-the-Wisp
entities.body: The zigzag light pressed into service as a guide up the Brocken, and told to go straight for once.

entities.name: Lilith
entities.body: Adam’s first wife, dancing on the Brocken; Mephistopheles warns Faust about her beautiful hair.

entities.name: Squire Voland
entities.body: The old German name for the devil, which Mephistopheles uses to clear a path through the crowd on the mountain.

entities.name: The General
entities.body: One of four has-beens sitting by the dying embers on the Brocken, complaining that the world has passed him by.

entities.name: The Minister
entities.body: A second of the four by the embers, who remembers when merit still counted.

entities.name: The Fair One
entities.body: The young witch Faust dances with, whose song about the apple tree he answers in kind.

entities.name: The Old One
entities.body: The old witch who dances with Mephistopheles and matches his coarseness.

entities.name: The Proktophantasmist
entities.body: Goethe’s caricature of a living critic who denied ghosts in print; he turns up on a mountain full of them and complains that they will not obey the rules.

entities.name: Servibilis
entities.body: The busybody who announces the amateur theatricals about to begin — the Walpurgis-Night’s Dream.

entities.name: Medusa
entities.body: Whose name Mephistopheles gives to the pale girl Faust cannot look away from — the vision with a red thread round her throat.

entities.name: Perseus
entities.body: Named for having cut off the head the vision carries under her arm.

entities.name: The Demi-Witch
entities.body: One of the crowd toiling up the mountain, a hundred years behind the others.

entities.name: The Chorus of Witches
entities.body: The crowd streaming to the summit — the salve gives courage, a rag serves for a sail.

entities.name: The Wizards
entities.body: The male half of the procession, creeping along while the women go ahead.

entities.name: Oberon
entities.body: The fairy king of the intermezzo, celebrating his golden wedding; Goethe borrows him from Shakespeare and Wieland.

entities.name: Titania
entities.body: Oberon’s queen, reconciled with him for the golden wedding.

entities.name: Puck
entities.body: Shakespeare’s sprite, come whirling into the masque.

entities.name: Ariel
entities.body: The airy spirit of The Tempest, leading the song in the masque.

entities.name: The Herald
entities.body: Who announces the golden wedding of Oberon and Titania.

entities.name: The Orchestra
entities.body: The band of gnats, flies and frogs that accompanies the masque, tuning up and signing off.

entities.name: Solo
entities.body: A single voice in the masque’s chorus.

entities.name: The Spirit that is Fashioning Itself
entities.body: A half-made creature in the masque, all legs and no body yet.

entities.name: A Pair of Lovers
entities.body: Two figures slipping away from the masque into the dark.

entities.name: The Inquisitive Traveller
entities.body: The tourist who asks whether all this is masquerade, and recognises Oberon.

entities.name: The Orthodox
entities.body: Who sees no claws and no tail and concludes that, like the gods of Greece, this one is a devil too.

entities.name: The Purist
entities.body: The literary pedant who objects that the witches are not delicately enough drawn.

entities.name: The Young Witch
entities.body: Who says dress and paint are for the old, and rides naked.

entities.name: The Matron
entities.body: Who is too well-bred to quarrel, and hopes the young one rots.

entities.name: The Leader of the Band
entities.body: Who tries to keep the insects off the naked witch.

entities.name: The Weathercock
entities.body: Who faces one way and then the other in two consecutive speeches — Goethe’s joke about turncoats.

entities.name: The Xenien
entities.body: The stinging epigrams Goethe and Schiller had published together, appearing in the masque as insects.

entities.name: Hennings
entities.body: A journalist who had attacked the Xenien; he appears here as one of the pests.

entities.name: Musaget
entities.body: The name of Hennings’s journal, personified as a leader of muses who would rather lead witches.

entities.name: The Ci-devant Genius of the Age
entities.body: Another of Hennings’s journals, which claims the Brocken as the German Parnassus.

entities.name: The Crane
entities.body: Lavater, the physiognomist, who fishes in clear water and in muddy.

entities.name: The Worldling
entities.body: Who observes that the pious will ride any vehicle that is going their way.

entities.name: The Dancer
entities.body: Who hears a new company coming and takes it for distant drums.

entities.name: The Dancing Master
entities.body: Who watches the crowd caper and cannot make them keep time.

entities.name: The Fiddler
entities.body: Whose bagpipe unites the rabble as Orpheus’s lyre united the beasts.

entities.name: The Dogmatist
entities.body: Who is not to be shaken by criticism, and concludes that the devil must be something because he exists.

entities.name: The Idealist
entities.body: Whose fantasy is tyrannical tonight, so that if all this is himself, he is a fool.

entities.name: The Realist
entities.body: To whom the whole business is a torment, since for the first time he cannot trust his own feet.

entities.name: The Supernaturalist
entities.body: Who is delighted to be here, because if there are devils there must be good spirits too.

entities.name: The Sceptic
entities.body: Who follows the little flames about looking for treasure, and observes that doubt rhymes with devil.

entities.name: The Adroit
entities.body: One of the nimble spirits, dancing barefoot in the moss.

entities.name: The Awkward
entities.body: One of the clumsy spirits, who used to sponge on the world and now walks on his head.

entities.name: The Shooting Star
entities.body: A falling light, sprawling on its side in the grass.

entities.name: The Massive Ones
entities.body: The heavy spirits who tramp through at the end of the masque.

entities.name: Orpheus
entities.body: Named for the lyre that tamed the beasts, as the Fiddler’s bagpipe tames this crowd.

entities.name: God
entities.body: Named throughout by Faust, Margaret and Mephistopheles alike; in the Prologue he speaks as the Lord.

entities.name: Christ
entities.body: Risen in the Easter chorus that stops Faust’s hand on the poison cup.

entities.name: Satan
entities.body: The name the Witch greets Mephistopheles by, and is told not to use any more — the gentlemen have given it up.

entities.name: Mammon
entities.body: The wealth-god whose name Faust curses, and whose mountain glows on the Brocken.

entities.name: Solomon
entities.body: Whose key the Witch’s nonsense book parodies.

entities.name: The Chorus of Angels
entities.body: The Easter choir that sings Christ is arisen — which does not convert Faust but does keep him alive.

entities.name: The Chorus of Disciples
entities.body: The answering choir, weeping over their master’s happy lot.

entities.name: The Chorus of Spirits
entities.body: Mephistopheles’s invisible servants, who tell Faust he has smashed the world and invite him to build it again.

entities.name: The Voice from Above
entities.body: The last word of the play: Mephistopheles says Margaret is judged, and the voice says she is saved.
